inputs.name: eSummary
inputs.value: A tour of the node: DID-native authorship, the draft→published lifecycle, the economy, the network, and the agent surface.

inputs.name: eBody
inputs.value:
# Hello ArcBlog

ArcBlog is a DID-native publishing space: a **Blocklet** that runs on the Arc
stack, keeps every story in the Arc File System, and binds authorship to a wallet
instead of a password. This first post is a tour of what the node can do.

## What it is

ArcBlog is not a hosted blog service and not a static site generator. It is a
self-contained node you run yourself:

- **Content** lives as Markdown-first records in AFS, one JSON record per story.
- **Identity** comes from DID Wallet. There is no separate account database —
  the wallet *is* the account.
- **The public site** is rendered from those records; nothing is duplicated into
  a CMS database.

Because the records are the product, everything else — the editor, the feed, the
RSS file, the agent surface — is a view over the same data.

## The content model

One schema, two directories, and a deliberate lifecycle:

| Stage | Where it lives | Who can read it |
|---|---|---|
| Draft | `drafts/` | Administrators only |
| Published | `posts/` | Everyone |
| Archived | `drafts/` | Administrators only |
| Deleted (soft) | `drafts/` | Administrators only |

`draft → published → archived → published` are all reversible; deleting is a soft
delete that keeps the record. The split is not cosmetic: the public directory is
guest-readable and the private one is not, so an unpublished draft can never leak
through a URL.

## Authorship you can verify

Every published story carries an `authorDid`. When you write from the studio, the
record is stamped with the wallet that signed in (`$session.did`); when you write
from the CLI you pass `--author-did` explicitly. Run

```bash
node scripts/arcblog-doctor.mjs
```

to audit the node: resource layout, identity records, taxonomy, and any story
whose authorship is missing.

## The public surface

`/posts` is the feed, `/posts/{slug}` is the reader, `/author` describes who
publishes here, and `/p/rss.xml` is the feed for readers who prefer a reader.
Categories and tags are data, not hard-coded strings — the taxonomy is stored in
AFS and the publish validator checks against it.

## An economy, not just a page

The node ships with a small, honest economy:

- a **versioned split policy** (creator / hub / protocol) that always adds up;
- **tips** for a story you liked, and **paid reading** for one you want to sell;
- an **append-only ledger** with deterministic entry ids, and access grants that
  are written only after a payment is verified;
- **signed discovery proofs**: a hub earns a share only when it can prove it sent
  the reader, verifiable offline against its public key.

Payments and payouts are separate steps on purpose. Nothing settles on an
unverified payment, and no hub is paid on an unverified claim.

## A network of nodes

A node is both a **Studio** (where you publish) and a **Hub** (where you curate).
Nodes publish a discovery document, register the hubs they work with, and track
sync state — all as AFS records, so the same data is reachable from the CLI, the
admin console, and an agent.

## Agents are first-class readers

The runtime already exposes an agent surface (MCP, AFS RPC). ArcBlog declares what
an agent may touch instead of inventing a protocol: a read-only agent over
published stories, taxonomy, the node profile and the public economy data — with
the write tools closed by default.

## Run it yourself

```bash
node scripts/arcblog-lifecycle.mjs publish --title "My story" \
  --author-did did:key:z... --body-file story.md --category technology

node scripts/arcblog-economy.mjs policy show
node scripts/arcblog-network.mjs health
node scripts/arcblog-agent.mjs check
```

That is the whole idea: your words, your identity, your node — and every layer
above it is just a view.
